title: The Hithpael

objectives.can: Recognise and parse Hithpael forms, including those where the ת changes place.

explanation.summary: The Hithpael puts the prefix hit- before a root whose middle consonant is doubled, like the Piel. Its commonest sense is reflexive, but it is also used for repeated or continuing action and, for some verbs, it is simply the ordinary form. When the root begins with a sibilant or a dental, the ת of the prefix changes place or is absorbed.

sections.heading: The shape of the Hithpael
body: The Hithpael has the Piel's doubled middle consonant and adds a prefix that ends in ת. In the qatal the prefix is הִתְ: הִתְפַּלֵּל. In the yiqtol the person prefix comes first and the ת follows it: יִתְפַּלֵּל. In the participle the prefix is מִתְ: מִתְפַּלֵּל. The imperative and the infinitive construct have the qatal's front: הִתְפַּלֵּל, לְהִתְפַּלֵּל. Before an ending that begins with a consonant the last vowel shortens: הִתְפַּלַּלְתָּ.
So there are two ways to find a Hithpael: the ת-prefix after the person letter, or the הִתְ at the front. Look then for the doubled middle consonant.

sections.heading: When the ת moves or changes
body: If the first root consonant is a sibilant (ס, שׁ, שׂ, צ), the ת and that consonant change places: the participle of the root 'hide' is מִסְתַּתֵּר, and the yiqtol of the root 'keep' is וְיִשְׁתַּמֵּר. With צ the ת also becomes ט: נִּצְטַדָּק in Genesis 44:16, 'we shall clear ourselves'.

If the first root consonant is a dental (ט or ד, and sometimes others), the ת is absorbed into it and that consonant is doubled: תִּטַּמָּאוּ in Leviticus 11:24, 'you will make yourselves unclean', beside the Qal יִטְמָא in the same verse; and מִדַּבֵּר, a participle of the root 'speak'. The prefix is then no longer visible as ת, and the doubled first consonant is the clue.

sections.heading: What the Hithpael does to the sense
body: The usual description is reflexive: the subject does the action to or for itself. Exodus 19:22 says that the priests 'must consecrate themselves' with a Hithpael of the root that gives the Piel 'consecrate' in Genesis 2:3; וַיִּתְחַבֵּא in Genesis 3:8 is 'he hid himself'.

For some verbs the Hithpael describes action that goes on or goes to and fro. The Qal of 'go' is common; the Hithpael מִתְהַלֵּךְ in Genesis 3:8 is 'walking about' in the garden. Some Hithpaels are reciprocal, or mean 'act as, show oneself as' something. And for a number of verbs the Hithpael is simply the ordinary form: הִתְפַּלֵּל, 'pray', in Genesis 20:17 is the verb in the form in which it is mostly found. As with every stem, the lexicon decides.

sections.heading: Hithpael and Niphal
body: Both stems can be reflexive. In Genesis 3:8 a Hithpael says that the man and his wife hid themselves, and in Genesis 3:10 a Niphal of the same root says that the man hid himself. Grammarians sometimes distinguish them by saying that the Hithpael stresses the subject's own activity, but this is a tendency and not a rule; do not expect it to settle a reading.

misunderstandings: The Hithpael is not always reflexive. It can describe continuing action, be reciprocal, or be the ordinary form of the verb.
The prefix is not always הִתְ in that order. After a sibilant the ת stands after the first root consonant, and after a dental it disappears into a doubled consonant.
The Hithpael is not a passive. The passive partner of the Piel is the Pual; the Hithpael has none of its own.
The doubled consonant of the Hithpael is the middle root consonant, as in the Piel. When a dental root absorbs the ת, the first consonant is doubled as well.

deeper.heading: Reflexive prefix
body: The ת of the Hithpael is generally explained as a reflexive element also seen in related Semitic languages, so that the stem was originally a reflexive of the Piel. That is the standard explanation of its history; the sense of any particular Hithpael is read from the verse.

The Hithpael is reflexive: 'you will make yourselves unclean'.
